sections.title: Welcome to the work
paragraphs: Welcome. In this first part, we will look at something you already know: how you usually approach a conversation, a decision, or a piece of work. The habits you rely on have helped you get things done. They can also shape what you notice and what you expect from other people.

This learning is voluntary. You can pause, return to a section, follow the example with us, or think about a process you know. If you choose to make notes, keep names, case details, and other private information out of them. You do not have to share a personal story to take part.

Across these lessons we will follow one work example. A division team is revising how people hear about and respond to a planning opportunity. There is a purpose and a decision deadline. The team has not yet settled on the best way to communicate, invite input, or explain what happened afterward. You can imagine yourself helping with a notice, a meeting, a recommendation, or another part of that work.

sections.title: The familiar can feel neutral
paragraphs: Imagine that the team usually shares a long draft the morning of a meeting and asks for reactions before the meeting ends. Some people find the discussion useful. Others may need a different way to review or respond. At this point, we do not know who prefers what or why.

You might be comfortable thinking out loud. You might prefer to read first, ask questions afterward, or have time to consult someone. A preference can change with the task, the amount of information, the people involved, and the time available. It is not a permanent label for you or anyone else.

The useful question is not whether one style is right. Ask what the work needs, what the current routine assumes, and which arrangements would give people a usable opportunity to contribute. A format can be familiar to the team without being required for the decision.

sections.title: Separate what happened from what you assumed
paragraphs: Suppose a participant says they would like more time before commenting. What do you know? You know they asked for more time. You may also know the decision date. You do not yet know why the person asked, what they might contribute, or whether an adjustment is possible.

An assumption might sound like, “They are not interested,” or “They are not prepared.” Another assumption could be, “Everyone who prefers written comments thinks the same way.” Each moves beyond the information you have. A more useful next step is to ask what would help and check what the team can offer.

This is also a chance to notice your own reaction. Perhaps you feel pressure because the deadline is close. That feeling is worth noticing, and it does not have to settle the question. You can acknowledge the constraint and still look for an option that respects the person's participation.

sections.title: Notice authority and impact
paragraphs: The team may have some choices and not others. A decision date, a review step, an accessibility requirement, or a policy may need confirmation. Within those limits, staff may have discretion over how clearly they invite comments or how people can ask for support. Check rather than assume which is which.

Roles matter too. A person who drafts an invitation may be able to suggest a change but not authorize a new deadline. A supervisor or another the person or area responsible may need to decide. The person affected is the best source for what would make their participation workable; their preference still needs an honest response about what is possible and what must be checked.

The goal is not to judge a colleague's intent. A team can mean to welcome everyone and still have a routine that is easier for some people to use than others. Looking at the effect gives you a practical place to begin.

sections.title: Try a decision
paragraphs: Return to the planning invitation. A participant asks for more time to review the draft. The decision date is approaching, and you have not yet confirmed whether the comment period can change. What would you do first?

Pause here if you would like to consider your response. Choose an answer in the activity, then compare the reasoning. You can revisit the choices and change your answer. The activity is practice; the actual requirements and decision authority belong to the people or areas responsible.

sections.title: Carry the question forward
paragraphs: Choose one small routine in your own work, or stay with the planning example. Name the step, what it is meant to accomplish, and one expectation it makes about the person using it. Then write a question that could help you check that expectation.

For example: “We usually ask for comments in a live meeting. What other response routes could fit the decision schedule, and whom should we ask before choosing?” You do not need to name a person or describe a private situation. The point is to make the next conversation more useful.

In the next part, we will look at the Minnesota community briefs as one source of context. We will use them to prepare better questions while keeping the answer with the individual and the people affected by the work.

practice.question: A participant asks for more time to review the planning draft. The decision date is approaching, and you have not confirmed whether the comment period can change. What would you do first?

options.text: Ask what would make participation workable, check the actual decision constraints and available response options, and bring the question to the person who can decide.
options.feedback: This starts with the person's request and checks both the room for adjustment and the responsible decision process. Explain what you learn and when you will follow up.

options.text: Promise to extend the comment period immediately, then tell the team afterward.
options.feedback: The request deserves a timely response, but a promise made before checking the deadline and decision authority may not be one you can keep. Ask what would help and seek the needed review.

options.text: Keep the meeting as the only response route because the team has used it before, and offer to summarize the draft afterward.
options.feedback: A summary may be useful, but it does not address the request to participate before the decision. Check whether other ways or times to contribute are available and explain any actual constraints.

practice.reflection: What is one expectation in a routine you touch, and what would you ask to find out whether it makes the work easier or harder for people?
practice.artifact: A general description of the step, its purpose, one assumption to check, and the person or office that can clarify the available options.

modules.title: Use context without making a profile

sections.title: Start with a better question
paragraphs: In the last part, we noticed how a familiar routine can carry an assumption. Now we will add context without turning that context into a prediction about a person.

The Minnesota Communities collection brings together history, place, contributions, experiences, and questions for work. The material can help you prepare, notice a possible access barrier, and find ideas for respectful questions. It does not tell you what an individual believes, what language they use, whom they trust, or what they want you to do.

You may explore a brief that is relevant to your work or simply follow the example. You are not expected to read the entire collection. Each person and each situation deserves attention in its own right.

sections.title: Read for context, then check the source
paragraphs: Imagine that you are helping prepare the planning invitation. You open a community brief before discussing the invitation with people affected by it. A passage describes a historical experience or a possible obstacle to using a public service. That gives you a reason to ask whether the current process creates a similar barrier. It does not establish that the person you will meet has encountered it.

Look at where a statement comes from and when it was written. A statistic may describe a particular place, period, definition, or group of respondents. A book offers an author's perspective. A community account may describe a real experience without representing every person in that community. If the source or its date is unclear, record the uncertainty and seek a current, appropriate source before repeating the claim.

You do not have to turn every unknown into a question for the person receiving a service. Ask only what helps with the work. Do not ask someone to explain their community, faith, immigration history, or a painful experience simply to satisfy your curiosity.

sections.title: Turn a description into an invitation
paragraphs: Suppose a brief discusses relationships and support. A rushed conclusion would be, “This person will want their family to decide.” A better question is, “Is there anyone you would like involved, and how would you like them to participate?” The question leaves room for a relative, a friend, a professional supporter, or no one else.

The same habit applies to language. A person's name, appearance, community, or country of origin does not tell you which language or communication method they prefer. Make it easy for everyone to request support, and ask what works for the individual when that information is needed.

There is variety within every community, and people may identify with more than one community or with none of the labels in a directory. Let the person describe what matters to them. When the brief raises a question about the way your team works, examine the process as well as the conversation.

sections.title: Context belongs beside accountability
paragraphs: Culture is not the only possible explanation for a barrier. A short response period, inaccessible document, missing interpretation, unreliable technology, transportation, workload, or unclear decision process may also affect participation. Start with what you can observe and the information people are willing to share; do not use a cultural label as a shortcut.

In the planning example, the team might learn that a notice is difficult to use. The useful follow-up is to ask what made it difficult, what would help, and who can review a change. Explain what is open to change and how feedback will be considered. If an answer is not yet known, say so and identify a next step.

For substantive questions concerning Native American individuals, communities, or Tribal Nations, follow this program's standing deference to the Office of Indian Affairs and the DHS offices responsible for Tribal relations and consultation. A general reading or listening activity does not replace a Nation's authority or government-to-government consultation. Seek the appropriate guidance rather than inventing an answer.

sections.title: Try a decision
paragraphs: A colleague reads that some people may value involving trusted supporters. The colleague proposes inviting a participant's relatives to the planning discussion before asking the participant. What would you do first?
Pause and choose an answer in the activity. Then read the explanation. Notice the difference between preparing an inclusive option and deciding for someone who should be involved.

sections.title: Carry a question forward
paragraphs: Choose one sentence or idea from an available brief, or use the example you just heard. Write down what it helps you notice, one question you could ask about the actual work, and one thing you do not yet know. Keep any note general and free of identifying or confidential information.

You can follow the source links or an existing reading for deeper context. Treat the source as a starting point, not a substitute for listening. Next we will use the same approach to make communication and participation more accessible.

practice.question: A colleague reads that some people may value involving trusted supporters and proposes inviting a participant's relatives to the planning discussion before asking the participant. What would you do first?

options.text: Ask the participant whether they want anyone involved and how they want that person to participate; check any applicable requirements.
options.feedback: This turns context into a person-led question. It leaves the choice with the participant while recognizing that actual decision roles or requirements may need to be checked.

options.text: Invite the relatives but explain that the participant can ask them to leave if the arrangement is uncomfortable.
options.feedback: Offering support can be helpful, but inviting people before asking gives away a choice that belongs with the participant. Ask first and clarify the role the participant wants them to have.

options.text: Hold the discussion with the participant alone because a private conversation is always the most independent approach.
options.feedback: Privacy and individual choice matter, but deciding alone for the participant is another assumption. They may prefer support, a private conversation, or a combination; ask them.

practice.reflection: What is one idea from a brief that could help you ask a more useful question, and what can it not tell you about an individual?
practice.artifact: One context note with its source and date, an open question for the work, and one uncertainty to check without identifying a person.

sections.title: Begin with the person and the task
paragraphs: Our planning team is ready to improve the invitation. The goal is not just to send a message. It is for people to receive information they can use, understand what they are being asked, and have a workable way to respond.

Think about the whole exchange: the invitation, the material someone needs to review, the conversation, the way they can ask for help, and the follow-up. A change to one step may not solve a barrier in another. The person using the process can tell you what is and is not working for them.

This lesson is voluntary and individual. You may use the shared example or a general process from your work. Keep any notes free of names, case details, health information, and other confidential information.

sections.title: Ask without guessing
paragraphs: The team has prepared a written notice in English and is considering what other support to offer. Rather than assigning a need from someone's name, background, age, disability, or the community brief you read, make the request process easy to find and ask the person what works for this communication.

An open question could be, “What language or communication format would help you take part?” Depending on the situation, another question might be, “Would you like an interpreter or another communication support, and how should we arrange it?” Ask about a practical need; do not demand a personal history as the price of access.

Listen to the answer and check that you understood it. If an arrangement is already documented in an approved process, use it appropriately so the person does not have to repeat the same request unnecessarily. If you cannot arrange a requested support yourself, explain whom you will contact and when the person can expect an update.

sections.title: Language assistance and accessible communication
paragraphs: Language assistance and disability access can overlap, but they are not identical. Someone may ask for an interpreter, a translated document, an accessible electronic file, a different way to communicate in a meeting, or more time with a communication device. The right arrangement depends on the person, the information, and the situation.

The National CLAS Standards call for language assistance at no cost to individuals in health and health care, notice of available assistance, and competent people providing it. The Department of Justice's effective-communication guidance describes aids and services for people with communication disabilities and the importance of the person's usual method and the context. Apply the relevant agency procedures and current requirements to your work; ask the person or area responsible when you are unsure. A short learning activity does not decide a legal obligation for every situation.

Do not assume that a relative, a child, or a bilingual colleague should interpret. Follow the applicable process for qualified assistance and privacy. If a person invites a supporter, ask what role they want that person to have; a supporter's presence does not automatically replace the person's own participation.

sections.title: Follow the invitation through
paragraphs: Return to the planning opportunity. A person tells the team that the current materials do not work with their communication method. Start by asking what would make the materials and conversation usable. Confirm what support is needed, who can arrange it, and when it will be ready. Check both the document and the meeting, not just one of them.

Make the next step clear. The team might provide an accessible version, arrange a qualified service, offer a usable way to send a response, or consult the appropriate accessibility or language-access contact. Which steps fit depends on the actual request and applicable procedures. Do not promise an arrangement you have not confirmed; do not leave the person to solve the problem alone.

Afterward, ask whether the arrangement worked and what remains difficult. Record only what is needed and allowed by the applicable process. A useful record helps the next step happen; it is not a collection of personal cultural stories.

sections.title: Try a decision
paragraphs: A participant says the projected captions at a planning meeting are not usable for them. The meeting organizer has not asked what alternative would work. What would you do next?
Pause and choose an answer in the activity. Then compare the explanations. Consider what you know about the participant's request and what you would need to check before deciding.

sections.title: Take one access check into your work
paragraphs: Choose an invitation, notice, meeting, or form you can influence, or continue with the example. Write down how someone can request language or communication support; what must happen before they participate; and who can help if you cannot resolve the request. Add one way to check whether the arrangement actually worked.

Use the existing access checklist and CLAS learning when you need more detail, and confirm current agency procedures. Next we will focus on the person's voice and on the relationships they choose to include in a decision.

practice.question: A participant says the projected captions at a planning meeting are not usable for them. The organizer has not asked what alternative would work. What would you do next?

options.text: Ask what communication and material arrangements work for the participant, arrange appropriate support through the applicable process, and confirm the next step.
options.feedback: This begins with the participant's actual needs and follows through on both the meeting and materials. If you cannot arrange support yourself, identify the responsible contact and keep the person informed.

options.text: Send the transcript afterward and continue the meeting, because the information will eventually be available in writing.
options.feedback: A transcript can be useful, but providing it only afterward may not give the person a usable way to participate in the meeting itself. Ask what arrangement works and check the appropriate procedure before proceeding.

options.text: Choose a different communication aid based on the participant's disability label and tell them what has been arranged.
options.feedback: A different aid might help, but a label does not establish which method works for this person and this exchange. Ask, use the responsible access process, and confirm the arrangement.

practice.reflection: How can someone request communication or language support in a process you touch, and how would you find out whether the arrangement worked?
practice.artifact: A general access check identifying the request route, the person or office responsible for arranging support, and a follow-up question.

modules.title: Put the person's voice and choices first

sections.title: Begin with the person
paragraphs: Welcome back. So far, you have considered the lens you bring, used community context to prepare questions, and looked at communication and access. Now let us bring those ideas into one conversation: how do we make room for the person who will live with the decision?

Our continuing example is a planning opportunity. A division team knows what the opportunity is for and when a decision is due. It is still working out how to explain the invitation, how people can respond, and what the responsible decision maker can consider. No single format or personal preference has been decided in advance.

A person-centered approach does not mean the staff member can promise every requested change. It means the person has a meaningful chance to understand the opportunity, say what matters to them, and take part in ways that work for them. Your role is to make the process clear, listen, and follow through on what you can do. When a requirement or decision belongs to another office, say so and identify the right route.

sections.title: Ask about support without assigning a role
paragraphs: Imagine a participant says they would like a trusted supporter to join a conversation and would also like some private time before responding. The supporter might be a relative, friend, advocate, or another person the participant chooses. Their relationship alone does not tell you what role the participant wants them to have.

You might begin: “Would you like your supporter here for the whole discussion, or for part of it? What would you like to talk through privately?” Give the person time to answer in their preferred way. Speak to them directly, provide appropriate communication support, and avoid directing every question to the supporter merely because that person is present.

Ask what the supporter is invited to do. They may help the person prepare questions, provide information the person wants shared, or offer another kind of support. Do not assume they make the decision. If a legal representative or another formal arrangement may affect the process, follow the applicable procedure and seek the appropriate guidance. Explain the roles that actually apply without guessing from a relationship or label.

sections.title: Make participation usable
paragraphs: A good invitation makes it easier to decide whether and how to take part. Explain the purpose in plain language, the time available, what is still open to influence, and how a person can respond. Ask what language, format, communication support, timing, or other access arrangements would be helpful. Arrange support through current procedures and check whether it works for the person.

When the participant asks for private time, discuss the available options and the timing honestly. For example, the person might want a break during a meeting or time afterward to consider an accessible copy of the information. Check which arrangements are available and whether there is a decision deadline. If you cannot offer the requested timing, explain the constraint and seek an appropriate alternative rather than presenting the limitation as the person's fault.

Be clear about privacy without making promises you cannot keep. Explain how information will be used and any applicable limits, using current guidance. For this learning activity, you do not need to record a participant's name, health information, case details, or reasons for choosing support. A general note such as “check the available private response options” is enough.

sections.title: A choice to consider
paragraphs: Consider the participant who wants a trusted supporter at the conversation and private time before responding. Three possible responses are available on this page. Choose the one you would take first, then explore the feedback. You can pause the video while you decide.
Consider what each response would mean for the participant and the planning process. Once you make a choice, the feedback will explain its effects.

sections.title: Carry the choice into your work
paragraphs: Think of a meeting, notice, or planning conversation connected to your work. Where does the process let a person say whom they want involved? Where could it make private thinking time or another response route clearer? If you are not responsible for the process, identify a question to bring to someone who is.

Write a general action rather than personal information. You might note: “Ask how the person wants a supporter involved, confirm available private response options, and explain the decision deadline.” If a question involves a specific case or protected information, use your organization's approved channels instead of these learning notes.

sections.title: Connect and continue
paragraphs: The existing CLAS learning and planning worksheet offer ways to consider communication, access and participation together. The access checks in the Library can help you examine whether a meeting, information, or response route can actually be used. These resources support your judgment; follow current program procedures and the person's stated needs.

In the next part, we will step back from one conversation and look at the process itself. A respectful interaction matters, and so does the way the notice, deadline, meeting, and response options work together for people who encounter them.

practice.question: A participant wants a trusted supporter at the conversation and private time before responding. What should you do first?

options.text: Ask the participant how they want the supporter involved, discuss the available private response options and explain any decision deadline.
options.feedback: This starts with the person’s choice, makes the available options clear and leaves any formal decision-making roles to the applicable process.

options.text: Ask the supporter to answer for the participant because the participant invited them.
options.feedback: An invitation to support does not by itself give someone decision-making authority. Speak with the participant and ask what role they want their supporter to have.

options.text: Require the participant to respond during the meeting so everyone receives the same amount of time.
options.feedback: The same immediate response rule may not provide a usable opportunity. Discuss available timing and access options, explain any deadline and seek review when an adjustment needs approval.

practice.reflection: Where can a person indicate whom they want involved and what time or support they need to respond?

modules.title: Look at the process as well as the encounter

sections.title: Step back and see the whole route
paragraphs: A good conversation can reveal a barrier. The next step is to ask whether the process itself makes that barrier more likely. In our continuing example, a team is revising how people hear about a planning opportunity and how they can respond. The purpose and deadline are known, while the choice of communication and participation methods is still open.

Imagine tracing the experience from beginning to end. A person receives or discovers an invitation, works out what it means, considers whether they can participate, sends a response, and learns what happened next. Each step is connected. If the invitation is hard to understand, a convenient meeting time alone may not make the opportunity usable. If someone can attend but cannot influence the question, attendance alone is not meaningful participation.

You do not need to know everything about a community before you begin. Start with the process you can see. Describe what it asks people to do, what is known about how it works, and whose experience has not yet been heard. A community brief may help you prepare a better question; it cannot tell you whether a particular person received a notice or why they did not respond.

sections.title: Trace where effort falls
paragraphs: Suppose the current proposal offers one quick live meeting as the only way to give feedback. List what a participant would need to do: receive the invitation, understand it, find time, use the meeting format, and contribute while the meeting is taking place. Then consider what remains unknown. Do people need another language or format? Could work schedules, caregiving, transportation, technology, or the time needed to think affect participation? Which conditions are supported by evidence, and which are questions to ask?

Avoid assuming that any barrier applies to a person because of a community label. A live meeting may work well for some people and poorly for others within the same community. Ask people affected what would help, and make sure input reaches beyond the people the team already knows. Pay attention to who has the authority, time, and resources to change the process.

Also examine the team's side of the process. What will happen to responses, who will review them, and what can still change? Adding a new way to respond is useful only if it is usable and the team can consider the input within the actual decision process. Name limits honestly instead of promising a choice that is not available.

sections.title: Compare practical alternatives
paragraphs: A second response route might include an accessible written option, a telephone option, a supported conversation, or another method people identify as useful. These are possibilities, not automatic requirements or a promise that all can be offered immediately. Check accessibility, language assistance, privacy, the deadline and the program's current procedures before deciding what to recommend.

Compare the alternatives against the purpose of the opportunity. Who can use each option? What extra effort does it place on participants and staff? What evidence do you have, and what would you need to learn? If a change requires approval, bring a clear proposal to the responsible person. Do not treat a community description as a substitute for a required equity analysis or as authority to change a policy.

The Equity Analysis Toolkit can help organize the purpose, people affected, evidence, alternatives and review. Use the quick learning questions here as a starting point. If your work requires a particular DHS analysis or review, follow that process; participation in this course does not change an agency obligation.

sections.title: A choice to consider
paragraphs: The team has proposed one quick live meeting as the only way to provide feedback. Before the invitation is finalized, what would you do? Choose one of the three responses on this page, then explore the feedback. You can pause to think about access, the decision deadline and what is still open to change.
Consider what each option assumes and what it would leave the team able to learn. The feedback becomes available after you choose.

sections.title: Put the process on paper
paragraphs: Choose a notice, form, meeting, or decision route from your own work. You may also continue with the planning invitation. In a private working file, draw a short sequence of steps. For each step, note one question: what does a person need in order to use this step, and what evidence would tell us whether it works?

Keep the note general. Do not include names, case details, health information, or other protected information in these learning notes. Identify an uncertainty, a person or office with relevant responsibility, and one possible improvement to discuss. If you do not have authority to make a change, your useful action may be to bring a well-formed question to the person who does.

sections.title: Connect and continue
paragraphs: The Equity Analysis Toolkit offers a place to examine a decision, compare alternatives and prepare for review. The community engagement resources can help plan how people affected may contribute. The access checks can help you look at communication, meetings and materials. Use each tool's own instructions for saving or downloading; this lesson does not promise that those tools save information in the same way.

Next, we will focus on relationships and the right review. We will consider how to explain the purpose of engagement, follow through on what people share, and recognize when a different government-to-government process applies.

practice.question: A team proposes one quick live meeting as the only way to provide feedback. Before finalizing the invitation, what should you do?

options.text: Ask people affected and responsible partners about usable alternatives, then compare the options and seek the review required for any change.
options.feedback: This checks actual access needs and the decision deadline, and treats a proposed alternative as something to review rather than an already approved solution.

options.text: Keep the live meeting as the only route because a meeting is available to everyone.
options.feedback: Availability on paper does not show that the time, format, communication or access arrangements work for everyone. Learn about barriers before choosing the process.

options.text: Pick a response format based on a community brief and assume everyone in that community will prefer it.
options.feedback: A brief can help prepare respectful questions; it cannot establish an individual’s preference. Ask people and evaluate the actual options and requirements.

practice.reflection: Map one step in a process, an access question it raises, and who could help evaluate an alternative.

modules.title: Build relationships and seek the right review

sections.title: Make the purpose clear
paragraphs: A relationship is more than an invitation sent once. In our continuing planning example, the team is considering how people will hear about an opportunity and how they can respond. Before contacting anyone, be clear about the purpose, what the team can still change, who makes the decision, and when a response is useful. These details help people decide whether and how they want to participate.

It is also important to say what you do not yet know. If a decision has already been made, do not invite input as though every option remains open. If the team can change the wording of an invitation but not the statutory deadline, explain that difference. When you are unsure what can be changed, check with the responsible person before making a promise.

Participation in this learning is individual and voluntary. The workplace action you consider may involve responsibilities, partners or review beyond your role. Use the learning to prepare a thoughtful question and the appropriate next step, not to assume authority you do not have.

sections.title: Listen in ways people can use
paragraphs: Ask how people would like to receive information and what would make it possible to respond. Depending on the work, that may involve language assistance, accessible materials, a workable time, another way to contribute, or support for participating. Check what current guidance permits and what arrangements are available. Do not assume that everyone reached through the same organization shares one preference.

A community organization may offer valuable knowledge and relationships. Ask what role it wants and can take, and recognize that one partner cannot speak for everyone. Where appropriate and under the applicable process, plan for compensation, accessible participation and the time people need. Explain how their input will be considered and how the team expects to report back. If you cannot make a commitment yourself, identify who can answer before presenting it as settled.

Protect information appropriately. Explain the purpose of a request, how information will be used and any applicable limits, based on current procedures. For this lesson, your own notes can remain general. You do not need to record anyone's name, case information, health details, immigration status or other private information.

sections.title: Know when another process applies
paragraphs: There is an important distinction between an individual's choices, community engagement and government-to-government consultation. A person can tell you what support or communication works for them. Community engagement can help a team understand a range of experiences and shape an open decision. Neither automatically fulfills a government-to-government obligation.

The existing One DSD direction is to defer to the Office of Indian Affairs and the DHS offices responsible for Tribal relations and consultation for substantive matters concerning Native American individuals, communities or Tribal Nations. If a proposed action may have Tribal implications, contact the person or area responsible or liaison before planning engagement or consultation, and follow its guidance and the applicable process. Each Nation is a distinct sovereign government; a general community brief is not Nation-specific guidance.

You do not need to decide here exactly which consultation process applies. Recognize the potential implication, identify the person or area responsible, and ask how to proceed. Do not present a general listening session, an invitation to a community organization, or a brief you have read as a substitute for the designated process.

sections.title: A choice to consider
paragraphs: Suppose the planning opportunity may affect a Tribal Nation. A team is considering a general listening session and is unsure whether another process is needed. Which step would you take? Choose one of the three responses on the page, then explore the feedback. Pause if you would like to think about what you can decide and who is responsible for the review.
Consider what each option would mean for the team’s next step and the people or areas responsible. The feedback becomes available after you choose.

sections.title: Plan a relationship, not just an event
paragraphs: Return to your work question. Write a general plan with five items: the purpose; what people may influence; the responsible decision maker; the support needed for participation; and how the team will respond after hearing from people. Add any question you need to take to a person or area responsible or other responsible partner.

If you do not know whether compensation, an interpreter, a particular format, or another arrangement is available, mark it as something to confirm. Do not put someone's private circumstances in your learning note. The value of your plan is that it makes responsibilities and unanswered questions visible before an invitation goes out.

A relationship also needs follow-through. After a decision, tell participants what was considered, what changed, what did not change and why, as appropriate to the process. If some information cannot be shared, explain what you can say and where questions can go. People should not have to guess whether their contribution reached anyone.

sections.title: Connect and continue
paragraphs: The community engagement and connections resources offer planning questions about purpose, influence and reporting back. The Minnesota Communities collection provides background for preparing questions, while the CLAS learning and the Equity Analysis Toolkit offer ways to examine access and a decision together. Use the standing Tribal deference and current designated guidance wherever they apply.
In the final part, we will bring the work together. You will prepare a small action and review plan, then consider how to tell whether a change helped the people it was intended to reach.

practice.question: A proposed action may affect a Tribal Nation. The team is considering a general listening session and is unsure whether another process is needed. What should happen next?

options.text: Contact the person or area responsible in DHS responsible for Tribal relations or consultation, and follow the standing deference and guidance before planning the appropriate process.
options.feedback: The person or area responsible can advise on the applicable process and contacts. A Nation is a sovereign government, and a general listening session does not automatically satisfy a government-to-government obligation.

options.text: Hold a general listening session and record it as completed government-to-government consultation.
options.feedback: A general session can serve a different purpose, but it does not by itself establish that the designated government-to-government process has been followed.

options.text: Use a community brief to decide which Nation-specific consultation steps the team should perform.
options.feedback: The standing direction is to defer to the people or areas responsible and the appropriate Nation-specific process. A general brief cannot supply that guidance or replace consultation.

practice.reflection: For a work question, identify what is open to input, who can decide, what support participation needs and which office or partner can advise on the right process.

sections.title: Bring the work together
paragraphs: You have followed one question through the learning: how can a notice, conversation, meeting, or program decision work better for the people it affects? You have examined your own expectations, used community context to prepare questions, considered communication and access, and looked at both the person's choices and the process around them.

Our planning opportunity is still an example for you to work through. The team has a purpose and a deadline; which methods are available, what people prefer, and which changes will be approved depend on the actual situation. Do not treat a possible improvement as something that has already happened. Describe the proposal, the open questions and the review it needs.

A useful plan can be small. It might begin with one accessible invitation, a clearer way to respond, or a question for the person responsible for the decision. Your contribution may be to test an idea within your role, or to prepare evidence and bring it to a colleague with the authority to decide. Either way, make the next step clear and realistic.

sections.title: Prepare an action for review
paragraphs: Start by naming the purpose: what should be easier or more equitable, and for whom? Describe the process being considered and the people who may experience it. List what you know, where the information came from, and what you still need to learn. Consider the effect of the current approach alongside at least one feasible alternative.

Next, identify how people can participate, what communication and access arrangements need to be confirmed, and what information may be shared. State any possible burden or unintended effect you want to examine. For example, a new online response option could help some people while creating more work for someone who cannot use it. Do not assume a person's preferences from a name, language, disability, or community description; ask and follow the appropriate process.

Name who can review or authorize the proposed step, what decision is still open and when the team will return to it. If the work may have Tribal implications, follow the standing direction to contact the designated DHS Tribal relations or consultation office and the Office of Indian Affairs as appropriate. An individual learning activity or a general engagement event does not replace that process or any required analysis.

sections.title: Choose evidence that answers the question
paragraphs: Once an authorized change is in use, look for evidence that relates to its purpose. A count of invitations, attendance or responses can tell you about activity. It does not by itself show that people understood the material, could use the format, had influence, or experienced the process as more accessible.

Ask what information can be collected and shared under current rules, whose perspective is missing, and how to protect privacy. Consider whether a small number could identify someone. You might compare participation routes, review general comments, or ask whether materials were understandable, but do not collect information just because it is available. Choose measures that are appropriate to the work and the people involved.

Be honest about limits. A positive count may reflect several factors, and one response will not describe every person's experience. Where evidence is incomplete, say what remains uncertain and identify the next responsible question. Then return to the people who contributed with an appropriate account of what happened and what can still be considered.

sections.title: A choice to consider
paragraphs: Imagine that attendance at a planning session increased. Participants also say that the materials were hard to use and they do not know how their comments were considered. What would you recommend next? Choose one of the three responses on the page, then explore the feedback. Pause while you compare the attendance figure with the experience people reported.
Think about what each option would do with the information available. Once you make a choice, the feedback will explain its effects.

sections.title: Make a working plan
paragraphs: For your own practice, write a general plan with these prompts: purpose; decision or process; people affected; what is known; what remains unknown; communication and access; possible options and burdens; participation and appropriate partners; responsible review; the next step; and a date or occasion to check back. You can adapt the plan to the work you actually do.

Keep the learning note free of names, case details, health information, religious affiliation, immigration status, personnel information and other protected information. If you need to work with a real person's information, use the approved systems and procedures for that work. Follow the page's actual instructions about whether a note is saved or needs to be downloaded; the learning materials do not change your organization's records requirements.

A plan is not complete simply because the boxes are filled in. Revisit it when a person offers a different experience, when the decision changes, or when a person or area responsible provides further guidance. If the evidence shows a new barrier, explain it and take the next step within your role.

sections.title: Continue the learning in your work
paragraphs: The community briefs remain available when you need background and better questions. The intercultural learning journey offers further reflection. The CLAS materials support attention to communication and access, while the Equity Analysis Toolkit and community engagement resources help connect learning to a decision and follow-through. Use a brief as context, never as an answer about an individual.

Before you leave, choose one next step you can take or one question you can bring to the right person. It does not have to solve the whole problem. A careful question, a usable invitation, a clear explanation, or an honest return conversation can make the next decision more thoughtful and more responsive to the people it affects.

practice.question: Attendance at a planning session increased, but people say the materials were hard to use and they do not know how comments were considered. What would you recommend?

options.text: Examine the access and follow-through concerns alongside the attendance count, then propose a reviewed next step and a way to report back.
options.feedback: The count describes participation activity; the concerns identify questions about usability and influence. Use both, protect privacy and seek the appropriate review before promising a change.

options.text: Treat higher attendance as proof that the process was accessible and responsive.
options.feedback: Attendance alone cannot establish whether people could use the materials or whether their input influenced the decision. Examine the concerns and any other appropriate evidence.

options.text: Assume the concerns reflect one community’s cultural preferences and choose a solution on their behalf.
options.feedback: Community context cannot explain an individual’s experience or replace asking what would help. Learn from the people affected and compare options within the actual decision process.

practice.reflection: Name one purpose, a useful question about access or influence, who can review a next step and when to check back.
